title: Sources tell WIRED a contractor linked a personal coding agent to a Pentagon network. Accenture says the claim has no merit
friendlyTitle: Sources say a contractor linked a personal coding agent to a Pentagon network. The company says that is not true
summary: WIRED reports that sources say an Accenture contractor connected a personal Claude Code account to a secure Department of Defense network used for controlled unclassified information, and that the agent then sent system details, including login credentials, to a third-party site. The sources say it ran for about two months. Accenture told WIRED the allegations were independently investigated and found to be without merit. The Department of Defense said it does not comment on the status of its networks. Anthropic pointed WIRED to a usage policy that bars using its products to bypass security controls without authorization.
friendlySummary: WIRED reports that unnamed sources say an Accenture contractor connected a personal Claude Code account to a secure US Department of Defense network, and that the agent then sent details about that system, including login details, to another website. The sources say this went on for about two months. Accenture told WIRED the claims were investigated on their own and found to have no merit. The Department of Defense said it does not comment on the state of its networks. Anthropic pointed to a rule that says its products must not be used to get around security controls without permission.
whyItMatters: The incident is disputed, so this is not a confirmed breach. The habit it describes is not in dispute: a personal coding agent does not belong on a work network, a client system, or anything that holds credentials. If your employer is pushing agents onto production systems, the question to ask first is whose account the agent is signed into, and where its output goes.
